Senses.Explanation: An abrupt exclamation, conventionally rendered “Bah!” In the Chan record it is a spoken action: a master inserts it before a rebuke, uses it alone as an answer, or directs it at a named interlocutor. The Stove-Breaker strikes the stove and says “Bah! This stove is only made of mud and tiles” (咄。此竈只是泥瓦合成); Danyuan says “Bah! Foolish fellow! Who is in the well?” (咄。癡漢。誰在井中); and one record answers “What is the Way?” (如何是道) simply with the exclamation before ordering the monk away. Its Chan deviation is this regular placement inside encounter dialogue as an answer or verbal blow, rather than merely narrative punctuation. The corpus gives the sound no further lexical gloss.
Senses.Note: The exact graph occurs 3,892 times in 343 allowlisted texts. It appears independently as rebuke, address, answer, and commentary interjection; no definition formula or morphological variant supplies a second lexical sense.

Occurrences.Kwic: 世尊咄曰。文殊。吾四十九年住世。未曾說一字。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Five Lamps Compendium retells Buddha addressing Manjusri: “Bah, Manjusri. In my forty-nine years in the world, I never said one word.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 以杖敲竈三下曰。咄。此竈只是泥瓦合成。聖從何來。靈從何起。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Stove-Breaker section: after striking the stove three times, he says, “Bah! This stove is only made of mud and tiles. Where does holiness come from? Where does efficacy arise?”

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧問。如何是道。師便咄。僧曰。學人未領旨。師曰。去。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An encounter preserved in the Five Lamps Compendium: asked “What is the Way?” the teacher immediately says “Bah!” and later “Go!”

Occurrences.Kwic: 耽源曰。咄。癡漢。誰在井中。仰山不契。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Blue Cliff Record raises Danyuan's reply: “Bah! Foolish fellow! Who is in the well?” The occurrence is in a retold case.

Senses.Explanation: Literally a “good knowing acquaintance,” this corpus-wide person label names a good teacher, guide, or good friend. The term occurs 2,832 times in 311 allowlisted texts. Dahui directly says, “those called good teachers guide all beings and cause them to see nature” (夫稱善知識者，引導一切眾生，令見佛性), then describes observing people's capacities and giving teaching as medicine matches illness. He calls such reception and guidance “the proper work a good teacher ought to do” (善知識本分合做底事), and elsewhere mentions “a good teacher's eye for distinguishing people” (善知識辨人眼). The Five Lamps Compendium describes travelling people “visiting good teachers” (參善知識). Another narrative has a student say, “a great good teacher is hard to encounter even across ages; now that I have met one, why begrudge body or life?” (大善知識歷劫難逢，今既得遇，豈惜身命). Asked “what is a good teacher?” (如何是善知識), Fohai replies that lanterns, pillars, cats, and dogs are all called good teachers. The same label supplies the vocative “Good friends!” when speakers address assemblies. Direct address changes who is being hailed, not the lexical kind of label.
Senses.Note: Dahui's role definition and Fohai's materially different answer are both retained, preventing an exclusively institutional or human-office definition. The former role/vocative targets applied the same label to people in referential and direct-address grammar and are merged. Compare accomplished person (作家), lineage teacher (宗師), visiting a good teacher (參善知識), general address (普說), and ascending the hall (上堂).

Occurrences.Kwic: 夫稱善知識者。引導一切眾生。令見佛性。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dahui's own record. He directly defines those called good teachers as guiding beings and causing them to see nature.

Occurrences.Kwic: 這箇是善知識本分合做底事。豈是彊為。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dahui calls receiving and maturing those who travelled to the gathering 'the proper work a good teacher ought to do,' not something forced.

Occurrences.Kwic: 如何是善知識。臣云。燈籠露柱猫兒狗子。皆稱善知識何必更問。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Continued Transmission of the Lamp narrates Fohai's report to the emperor of his exchange with Zeng Kai. Asked what a good teacher is, Fohai names lanterns, pillars, cats, and dogs. As a reported two-person exchange, MasterName is null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 凡行脚人參善知識。到一叢林。放下瓶鉢。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Five Lamps Compendium, Baozi Xingyan section. The master speaks of travelling people visiting good teachers and arriving at a community; no exact roster link is available.

Occurrences.Kwic: 非但失却善知識辨人眼。亦乃賺他百劫千生。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dahui's record names 'a good teacher's eye for distinguishing people' while criticizing acceptance of a person's presentation for irrelevant reasons.

Occurrences.Kwic: 善知識！一行三昧者，於一切處行住坐臥，常行一直心是也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In the Platform Record, Huineng addresses the assembly as “Good friends!” before defining complete command of the single conduct.

Occurrences.Kwic: 善知識！一言半句實有起死回生之力、翻窠倒臼之施
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A public address hails the assembly as “Good friends!” before speaking of a word or half a phrase. No exact roster link was assigned.

Occurrences.Kwic: 大善知識歷劫難逢。今既得遇，豈惜身命！
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A student says that a great good teacher is hard to encounter even across ages and, having now met one, asks why he should begrudge body or life.

Senses.Explanation: Literally “mysterious” or “dark purport”: “mysterious” (玄) modifies “purport” or “gist” (旨). The compound occurs 564 times in 162 allowlisted texts. It is repeatedly asked as “What is the mysterious purport?” (如何是玄旨), a formula found 39 times in 23 texts. Guizong Zhichang answers that no one can understand it, says that directing oneself toward it departs from it, and asks who is seeking it; Zhaozhou answers “money hanging on the wall” (壁上挂錢財); and Daoqin replies, “What purport does ‘mysterious’ have?” (玄有甚麼旨). Jiashan Shanhui gives an explicit reciprocal formulation: “Your mysterious purport is this old monk’s tongue; this old monk’s mysterious purport is your tongue” (闍梨玄旨是老僧舌頭，老僧玄旨是闍梨舌頭). The compound also occurs as the object of verbs of recognition: records say people “greatly awakened to the mysterious purport” (大悟玄旨) or “realized the mysterious purport” (領悟玄旨). The recorded answers are retained as distinct answers; the entry does not replace them with a single explanation of their force.
Senses.Note: The question formula occurs across many masters, and the answers differ. “Not recognizing the mysterious purport” (不識玄旨) occurs 48 times in 35 texts; “greatly awakened to the mysterious purport” (大悟玄旨) occurs 19 times in 14; and “realized the mysterious purport” (領悟玄旨) occurs 6 times in 6. These are grammatical deployments of the same compound, not separate master-specific meanings.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧問。如何是玄旨。師云。無人能會。僧云。向者如何。師云。有向即乖。僧云。不向者如何。師云。誰求玄旨。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The surrounding Guizong Zhichang record supplies the monk’s question and Guizong’s successive replies.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧問：如何是玄旨？師云：壁上挂錢財。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The governing Zhaozhou Congshen section identifies Zhaozhou as the respondent.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問：如何是玄旨？師曰：玄有甚麼旨？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The governing section is the record of Jinling Zhongshan Zhangyi Daoyin; the roster has no exact link value for this name.

Occurrences.Kwic: 闍梨玄旨是老僧舌頭，老僧玄旨是闍梨舌頭。坐却舌頭，別生見解。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The governing Jiashan Shanhui discourse section records Jiashan’s reciprocal formulation.

Occurrences.Kwic: 違順相爭。是為心病。不識玄旨。徒勞念靜。圓同太虗。無欠無餘。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: This is the line containing the headword in the Inscription on Trusting Mind under Sengcan’s section.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師默而審之。大悟玄旨。尋晦迹鍾山。多歷年所。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The governing Zhongshan Tancui biography records the phrase as a narrative event; the roster has no exact link value for Tancui.

Senses.Explanation: The graphs join “hidden” or “subtle” with a trigger, pivot, or working. Chan records use the compound for workings disclosed in sayings, gestures, and exchanges. One verse calls them “subtle workings and marvelous function” and immediately lists raising the whisk, lifting the eyebrows, and answering questions. Another stock line says that “subtle workings beyond the norms” seek one who knows; a verse warns that people who try to grasp what precedes the working violate it beneath the phrase. The corpus can also negate it: “the intent cuts off subtle workings” stands beside “the mind has no affairs” and “the myriad things do not arise.” The headword occurs 500 times across 187 allowlisted texts.
Senses.Note: The personal name Xuanji, borne by a nun in lamp biography, is a homonym and is excluded: lineage figures belong on the master roster, not in this lexical sense.

Occurrences.Kwic: 格外玄機為尋知己
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A stock hall-address line says that subtle workings beyond the norms seek one who knows.

Occurrences.Kwic: 玄機妙用縱多般，七縱八橫任抵對
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A verse couples subtle workings with marvelous function and the ability to answer in every direction.

Occurrences.Kwic: 禪者有玄機。機玄是復非。欲了機前旨。咸於句下違
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A verse says Chan people have subtle workings and warns that seeking the purport before the working goes wrong beneath the phrase.

Occurrences.Kwic: 心若無事。萬法不生。意絕玄機。纖塵何立
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A hall address explicitly speaks of intent cutting off subtle workings.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, 'the dark' or 'hidden road.' The term occurs 268 times in 116 allowed texts. It is especially prominent in Caodong records, where one text says Dongshan taught 'three roads' (三路): the hidden road, the bird road, and extending the hand (玄路、鳥道、展手). Asked, 'How does the hidden road receive people?' (如何是玄路接人), one master answers, 'Push father toward the inside' (推爺向裏頭). Another exchange asks, 'What is it that every line must travel the hidden road?' (如何是句句須行玄路); the answer is 'Follow the road straight to Hunan' (㳂路直到湖南). The named compound 'golden-lock hidden road' (金鎖玄路) has its own verse, whose lines say that brightness and darkness alternate, equal accomplishment makes turning difficult, and at the exhaustion of strength advance and retreat are forgotten. A later prose explanation calls the inability to turn when strength is exhausted 'the golden-lock hidden road' (若力窮而不能轉，是謂金鎖玄路). The term does not by itself mark completion: a later record says that even when host and guest are established and question and answer are voiced, raising the hidden road from the side is still only halfway. The corpus has ten occurrences each of 'open the hidden road' (開玄路) and the request 'please make the hidden road clear' (玄路請師明).
Senses.Note: The definition follows the graphs and the records' road imagery. The entry reports the named three-road grouping, questions, answers, verse, and explicit qualification without converting the road into an imported program or interpreting the recorded replies.

Occurrences.Kwic: 如何是玄路接人？師云：推爺向裏頭。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A direct question asks how the hidden road receives people; the answer says to push father toward the inside. The exchange remains unkeyed.

Occurrences.Kwic: 曰。何者三路。曰。玄路．鳥道．展手。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A student reporting Dongshan's instruction directly names the three roads: hidden road, bird road, and extending the hand; the two-speaker exchange remains unkeyed.

Occurrences.Kwic: 如何是句句須行玄路。師曰。㳂路直到湖南。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A direct exchange asks about every line traveling the hidden road; the answer says to follow the road straight to Hunan.

Occurrences.Kwic: 金鎻玄路偈曰。交互明中暗。功齊轉覺難。力窮忘進退。金鎻網鞔鞔。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The collection preserves a verse explicitly titled 'Golden-Lock Hidden Road.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 若力窮而不能轉，則事理之迹未消，聖凡之情未盡，是謂金鎖玄路。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later prose explanation directly calls exhaustion of strength without the ability to turn the golden-lock hidden road.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問答言陳，仍玄路旁提為唱。若能如是，猶在半途。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Strict Continuation of the Five Lamps. The record qualifies raising the hidden road from the side as still being halfway.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, a dark, hidden, or subtle barrier/gate. The expression occurs 593 times in 212 allowlisted texts. One penetrates, passes, strikes, breaks, or kicks it down. Speakers ask about ‘the higher hidden barrier,’ call for one who has passed it, and ask publicly how it is passed. One discourse warns that ‘clinging to the hidden barrier’ loses the larger function; another says those not through it often construe Bodhidharma’s wall-gazing merely as facing a wall. Zen bends the gate into a public-interview checkpoint, but no corpus-wide sentence defines fixed content behind it.
Senses.Note: Family check: ancestral, higher, and double hidden barriers are qualified versions of one checkpoint image. Place-name compounds were excluded; no split.

Occurrences.Kwic: 上堂：未開口時先分付，擬思量處隔千山。莫言佛法無多子，未透玄關也大難。祇如玄關作麼生透？喝一喝，下座。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A discourse asks publicly how it is passed.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧云：四賓主諙蒙師指，向上玄關事若何？師曰：一陣兩陣清風生，吹散白雲千萬片。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A monk asks about the higher hidden barrier.

Occurrences.Kwic: 戀著玄關，全虧大用；灰身滅智，豈是良圖？裂破面門，救諸苦趣；為祥為瑞，今正是時。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The text warns against clinging to it.

Occurrences.Kwic: 未透玄關者往往只作面壁會却。上堂，舉：僧問首山：如何是祖師西來意？首山云：風吹日炙。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: It is linked to a warning about construing wall-gazing.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧問：「結制安禪即不問，今朝解制事如何？」師云：「蹋倒玄關無障礙。」進云：「解制後又如何？」師云：「十方世界任逍遙。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An interview answer says to kick it down.

Occurrences.Kwic: 上堂：孤村陋店，莫挂瓶盂。祖佛玄關，橫身直過。早是蘇秦觸塞，求路難回。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A discourse names the buddhas’ and patriarchs’ hidden barrier.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, “do you yet understand?” In Chan records it is a recurring public-interview question after a master has spoken, displayed an object, stood up, or made another gesture. The addressee may answer “I do not understand”; a master may then speak again, request an object, or close the address. In hall discourse it also turns from an exposition to the assembly: “Do you get it? If not yet…” A long pause, a verse, a staff gesture, or the closing “take care” is frequently recorded after the question. The distinctive Chan deployment is therefore not a private report of comprehension but an observable demand made to an emperor, official, monk, or whole assembly in a recorded encounter.
Senses.Note: One interrogative formula; its different follow-up actions are deployment shapes, not different senses.

Occurrences.Kwic: 陛下還會麼。帝曰。不會。聖師曰。大士講經竟
Occurrences.AttributionNote: After Fu Dashi mounts the seat, strikes once with a ruler, and leaves, the imperial teacher asks the emperor, “Does Your Majesty get it?” The emperor says, “I do not.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 諸人還會麼。其或未然。更煩知音底人。為我說破
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Hongzhi asks the whole assembly, “Do you get it? If perhaps not yet, I will trouble one who knows the tune to explain it for me.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 還會麼？若也未會，拄杖子重說偈言去也。擊禪牀一下
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A hall address asks “Do you get it?” then says the staff will recite a verse again if not, followed by a strike on the Chan seat.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師乃起立曰。還會麼。曰不會。師曰。與老僧過淨瓶來
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In response to a question, the master stands and asks “Do you get it?”; after “I do not,” he asks for his water bottle.
